conclusion.justification: The report concludes that current scientific evidence does not conclusively show hypnosis to be effective for smoking cessation and explicitly states that rigorous clinical evidence does not substantiate its efficacy. Therefore, it rejects the claim as unsupported by evidence.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
### Conclusion

Current scientific evidence does not conclusively show that hypnosis is an effective aid for smoking cessation compared to unassisted quitting or standard behavioral support.

### Evidence Summary

* **Cochrane Systematic Review:** Comprehensive reviews of randomized controlled trials conclude there is insufficient evidence to determine whether hypnotherapy is more effective for smoking cessation than other forms of behavioral support or quitting without assistance. Any potential benefit, if present, appears to be small at most (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking; https://www.drugsandalcohol.ie/16580/).
* **National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH):** The NCCIH reports that clinical studies examining hypnosis for quitting smoking have yielded conflicting results. They note that there is currently not enough consistent evidence to demonstrate that hypnosis is more effective than other quitting aids or self-quitting (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/hypnosis; https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/quitting-smoking).

Although hypnosis remains a popular alternative therapy, rigorous clinical evidence does not currently substantiate its efficacy for stopping smoking.
